transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Um... well, I came in because I can’t seem to stop launching projects. It’s just constant. Work plans, certification schedules for my team... which, honestly, the new vendor we're using for the cybersecurity certs is a total nightmare. I spent half of Tuesday trying to explain to their support guy that their portal doesn't even sync with our single sign-on, which is basic stuff, you know? I mean, I've been an IT manager for a while, and the lack of standard integration these days is wild. 

But anyway, yeah, I'm just always starting things. Like home network upgrades. I was up in the attic running new cable last week and I found this old box of stuff from when I was getting my bachelor's, which got me sending messages to all these old contacts I haven't talked to in years. My old roommate actually lives in Denver now, apparently. But the thing is, doing all this... it gets so intense that I just blow past normal limits. Like, I don't even see it happening until my wife or my director at work has to finally step in and tell me to stop.

When you're in these periods where you're launching all these projects and pushing past your limits, do you also notice that your mood feels unusually elevated or energetic compared to your normal baseline—like you feel exceptionally good, confident, or like you need very little sleep?

Yeah, energetic is... yeah. Some weeks I feel almost electric, honestly. Just completely unstoppable. But then, if there's even a tiny delay, or my wife asks a simple question about what I'm doing, I just snap. It feels like everyone is trying to slow me down on purpose. 

Like, the other day she asked why I had the new mesh network nodes spread out all over the kitchen counter. And I'm just trying to optimize our Wi-Fi coverage, you know? Which we really need because our ISP is terrible. They promised gigabit speeds in our neighborhood two years ago and they still haven't laid the fiber on our street. I actually walked down to where they were trenching a few blocks over to ask the foreman what the hold up was, but he was just a subcontractor. It’s crazy how these big telecoms just outsource everything now. When I first got into tech, companies actually kept their infrastructure teams in-house. You actually knew the guys pulling the cables. Now it's just a race to the bottom for whoever bids lowest on the contract... 

Wait, what did you ask me? Something about sleep?

Besides these energetic periods where you're launching projects and feeling unstoppable, have you had other times—maybe lasting days or weeks—where your mood was the opposite: low, depressed, or hopeless?

Yeah, the opposite... yeah, definitely. There are these stretches where I wake up and I just feel like this... failed version of myself. It's just heavy and flat. Even answering my wife's normal questions feels like it takes too much energy. Which is tough because she’s a teacher, right? So she’s used to asking a lot of questions and keeping track of everyone. She teaches fourth grade, and honestly, the amount of administrative work they make teachers do now is insane. She brings home these massive binders of state standards she has to map her lessons to. I tried to build her a database to automate some of it—just a simple relational database, you know, link the lesson plans to the state codes. I spent a whole weekend setting up the schema, but the district’s IT department wouldn't let us install the client on her work laptop. They have it locked down so tight you can't even update the browser without an admin password. It's ridiculous, I mean, I get security, but you have to let people actually do their jobs... 

But yeah, I do get really low sometimes. Just completely drained.
When you're in one of those low, heavy, flat periods you described, how long do they typically last? Are we talking about a few days, or more like weeks at a time?

Um, well, if I look at the whole picture... like, since this all really started, those low, withdrawn periods have probably added up to about seven months total. Just chunks of time where I'm totally offline, you know? It's like my internal server just crashes and won't reboot. Speaking of servers, my team at work is actually migrating our entire backend to a new cloud provider next month. It's supposed to save the company like twenty percent on hosting costs, but the migration plan they handed me is a joke. They want us to do it in phases, which sounds smart on paper, but it means we have to maintain the legacy system and the new cloud infrastructure at the same time. The data redundancy alone is going to be a nightmare to manage. I told the VP of Engineering that we should just do a hard cutover over a holiday weekend. You know, rip the band-aid off. But he’s so risk-averse. He used to work at this old banking firm where everything moved at a snail's pace, so he still thinks we need to double-check every single packet of data... 

Sorry, what was I saying? Oh, right, the low periods. Yeah, they last for weeks at a time, adding up to around seven months overall.

During those energetic, electric periods you described—when you're launching all these projects and feeling unstoppable—have you ever had experiences like hearing voices, seeing things others didn't see, or believing things that turned out not to be true, even though they felt completely real at the time?

Yeah, actually... when I'm really pushing hard, like barely sleeping and just knocking out those huge plans, things get... weird. I started hearing these comments, like actual voices, just kind of buried in the hum of the servers at work. And the messages on Slack—I was totally reading these hidden threats into what my coworkers were sending me. Which is crazy because Slack is supposed to be this great collaboration tool, right? They really cornered the market early on, but honestly, Microsoft Teams has been eating their lunch lately because it comes bundled with Office 365. My company is actually talking about switching to Teams next quarter to save on licensing fees. It's going to be a huge headache for my department because we have all these custom API integrations built into Slack. We have this one bot that automatically pulls deployment metrics from GitHub and posts them in the dev channel, and rebuilding that for Teams is going to take weeks. I told them we should just stick with Slack, but management only looks at the bottom line, you know? They don't care about the technical debt they're creating...

But yeah, the voices in the server noise and the hidden messages... that definitely happened during those really driven stretches.

When you're in those electric, unstoppable periods—the ones where you're launching all these projects and barely sleeping—do those high-energy stretches typically last for at least a full week, or are they usually shorter than that?

Oh, definitely a week, usually way longer at a time. If you look at the whole timeline, those unusually driven, low-sleep, overconfident stretches have been a part of my life for roughly a year and eight months now. 

I know the exact timeline because a year and eight months ago is right when my company forced our whole division to switch to Agile methodology. Have you ever worked with Agile? It's supposed to make software development faster, but it just adds so much bureaucratic overhead. We have to work in these two-week "sprints" now, and they hired this Scrum master—this guy Dave, who used to be in marketing, by the way, so he doesn't even understand the backend architecture we're building. He makes us do these daily stand-up meetings at 9 AM sharp where we have to justify our existence and explain what we did yesterday. It's just micro-management disguised as productivity. And the Jira boards—don't even get me started on Jira. The permissions are set up so poorly by the enterprise team that half my engineers can't even move their own tickets to the "Done" column without my approval. So I spend half my day just clicking buttons so Dave's metrics look good for upper management. It completely ruins my flow state, you know? Especially when I'm actually trying to build something and I'm in the zone... 

But yeah, to answer your question, those high-energy stretches have been happening for about a year and eight months.

During those stretches when you were feeling electric and unstoppable for a week or more, did you have times when your mood felt so good, so expansive, or so confident that you actually got into serious trouble—like damaging relationships, losing money, getting fired, or doing something that had major real-world consequences?

Yeah, um, there have definitely been consequences. Like, major ones. When I was in that zone, pushing that big migration I mentioned? Well, it failed. Spectacularly. And they actually put me on administrative leave because of it. Which is ridiculous, honestly, because the failure wasn't even my fault—it was a DNS propagation issue with the new cloud provider. But do you think management understands how DNS works? No. They just see downtime and panic. It's like how my neighbor, Gary, tries to fix his own Wi-Fi. The guy is a retired dentist, and he bought this top-of-the-line mesh network system, right? But he set all the nodes right next to his microwave and his thickest brick walls. So he's constantly complaining to me over the fence about how his internet is "broken," and I keep trying to explain signal interference to him, but he just wants to call the ISP and yell at some poor customer service rep. He actually threatened to sue them once over a dead zone in his garage...

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, the consequences. Yeah, so I'm on leave. And at home, it's been... rough. My wife has had to step in big time. She's monitoring my spending, trying to stop my late-night coding sessions, and honestly, a lot of our conversations just turn into these massive arguments. And I've just kind of dropped everything else. I used to play music at church, go rock climbing, I was mentoring a junior dev... but I've pulled away from all of it. I just can't reliably show up or follow through on any of it right now.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a clear pattern of distinct mood episodes over approximately 20 months: (1) recurrent manic/hypomanic episodes lasting weeks or longer, characterized by elevated/expansive mood, decreased need for sleep, goal-directed overactivity, racing thoughts, irritability, and poor judgment leading to serious consequences (job loss via administrative leave); (2) depressive episodes lasting weeks at a time, totaling approximately 7 months, with anhedonia, fatigue, and withdrawal; (3) psychotic features (auditory hallusions, paranoid ideation about Slack messages) occurring specifically during high-energy periods. The timeline, biphasic course, functional impairment (job loss, marital strain, loss of social engagement), and psychotic symptoms limited to mood episodes are consistent with Bipolar I Disorder. While psychotic features are present, they are clearly mood-congruent and occur within the context of distinct mood episodes rather than representing independent psychotic illness.
